sections.h2: Which Jersey City offices handle property tax?
sections.html:
Jersey City splits the work between a Tax Assessor, who sets and records values, and a Tax Collector, who sends the bills and takes payment. The collector's counter is at 280 Grove Street, Room 101, and opens from 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. on business days. Mail goes to the City of Jersey City Tax Collector at that address, with checks or money orders made out to the same name. The city's property tax page also lists online payment and a bank-debit option that uses a signed authorization form.

The assessor's page tells owners how to look up an assessment: open the state-hosted tax records site, choose Hudson County and Jersey City, then search by street address, owner name or block and lot. The same page links the forms most sellers and heirs end up needing, including veteran deduction claims, exemption claims and the five-year exemption and abatement application.

One note on the city's separate tax page: it describes a payroll tax on employers, and resident wages are exempt. That levy is unrelated to your home.

sections.h2: What are the Jersey City property tax due dates?
sections.html:
The city lists four due dates: February 1, May 1, August 1 and November 1. They match the installment schedule in N.J.S.A. 54:4-66. Ask the collector what grace period applies to the current year before you rely on a date past the first of the month.

Jersey City installments and how each amount is set
InstallmentDue dateHow the amount is figured
FirstFebruary 1One quarter of the prior year's tax
SecondMay 1One quarter of the prior year's tax
ThirdAugust 1Half of the current levy left after the first two payments
FourthNovember 1The other half of that remaining current levy

Source: City of Jersey City property tax page; N.J.S.A. 54:4-66(a) and (c).

Any quarter unpaid after its delinquency date stays delinquent, with interest, until the taxes and liens due on the property are all settled. The statute also lets an owner pay early, and no interest builds until the delinquency date.

sections.h2: How high is the tax rate in Jersey City?
sections.html:
The Division of Taxation's 2025 table gives Jersey City a general rate of 2.335 and an effective rate of 1.847. The effective rate restates that levy against estimated full value, which makes it the fairer yardstick when you compare towns. Among the county's twelve municipalities Jersey City falls in the middle on the effective measure, higher than Hoboken at 1.070 and lower than Bayonne at 1.987.

The city's last full revaluation of every property took place in 2017, carried out in response to a state order. Assessments since then are updated by the assessor's office. For a seller, the practical step is to read the most recent assessment for your block and lot and compare it with what similar homes sold for nearby.

Source: NJ Division of Taxation, 2025 General Tax Rates; Jersey City revaluation page.

sections.h2: Can I appeal a Jersey City assessment?
sections.html:
Yes. Jersey City assessments are appealed to the Hudson County Board of Taxation, and the assessor's page links the county petition and its instructions. The filing date is April 1 each year, or 45 days after assessment notices are bulk mailed, whichever is later. After a municipal revaluation or reassessment the date is May 1. The county's appeal system accepts online filing, paper forms handed in at the office on Cornelison Avenue, or forms mailed on request through the board's phone line at (201) 395-6260.

  • Evidence should come from before the October 1 assessment date, because the board looks at the value as of that day.
  • Three to five comparable sales with photos are the standard attachments.
  • Showing up matters: a missed hearing can end in a judgment for lack of prosecution, which can block a later Tax Court appeal.
  • A lowered assessment is frozen for the year of appeal and two more years.

Source: NJ Division of Taxation guide to tax appeal hearings; Hudson County Division of Tax Assessments.

sections.h2: What is the Jersey City housing market like by the numbers?
sections.html:
Jersey City covers 14.74 square miles of land and counted 292,449 people in the 2020 census, with an estimate of 302,013 for 2025. That is about 19,835 residents per square mile. Only 27.9 percent of homes are owner-occupied. The median value of those owner-occupied homes was $566,900 for 2020 to 2024, median gross rent was $2,007, and median household income was $97,710.

The city has 125,223 households averaging 2.33 people. Foreign-born residents make up 41.7 percent of the population, and 50.9 percent of residents age five and older speak a language other than English at home. A seller here is usually dealing with a market where most neighbors rent, so a house with tenants is a common situation.

Source: Census Bureau QuickFacts.

sections.h2: How does the shape of Jersey City affect a house sale?
sections.html:
Jersey City is the second most populous city in New Jersey and the seat of Hudson County. The Hudson River and Upper New York Bay border it on the east, and the Hackensack River and Newark Bay border it on the west. It has about 30.7 miles of waterfront and a long history as a port and rail terminus. The city formed in 1870 by merging Jersey City, Hudson City and Bergen, and Greenville joined three years later.

Those layers produce distinct areas that buyers search by name: Paulus Hook and the downtown waterfront, Journal Square, Bergen Hill, the Heights and Greenville in the south. The waterfront has a flood record, since Hurricane Irene's storm surge flooded parts of downtown in August 2011. Flood exposure is worth checking on a waterfront or low-lying block before you price a sale or negotiate repairs. The city connects to Manhattan through the Holland Tunnel, PATH, NJ Transit buses and NY Waterway ferries.

Source: Jersey City, New Jersey (Wikipedia).

sections.h2: How should a seller handle tax owed on a Jersey City house?
sections.html:
Start with the assessment search so you know the block and lot on record, then ask the collector for the balance by quarter. Three items cause most surprises: a quarter that went delinquent, a tax lien held by a third party, and a bill for an abatement payment, which the city's payment page routes to its own portal. If the house has a five-year exemption or abatement, confirm that its payment is current before closing.

  • Bring the block and lot, the owner's name and the property address when you call the collector.
  • Ask for a written payoff figure good through the closing date.
  • Ask the assessor whether a veteran or senior deduction on the property ends with the sale.
  • Inherited houses may carry unpaid quarters from before the owner's death, so check them first.

faqs.q: What are the due dates for property tax in Jersey City?
faqs.a: They are February 1, May 1, August 1 and November 1. The collector can confirm the grace period that applies to each quarter.

faqs.q: Where can I pay a Jersey City property tax bill in person?
faqs.a: The Tax Collector's office is at 280 Grove Street, Room 101, and is open from 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. on business days. Payment is also available online or by mail with a check or money order.

faqs.q: How do I look up my Jersey City assessment?
faqs.a: Use the state-hosted tax records site linked from the assessor's page, pick Hudson County and Jersey City, and search by address, owner or block and lot.

faqs.q: When did Jersey City last revalue every property?
faqs.a: The city completed a full revaluation in 2017 in response to a state order. Assessments since then are maintained by the assessor's office.

faqs.q: Does a Jersey City appeal go to the city or the county?
faqs.a: It goes to the Hudson County Board of Taxation. The filing date is April 1, or 45 days after bulk mailing of notices if that is later, and May 1 after a revaluation.
